questions.question: What does the Arabic term 'al-takathur' refer to in the opening verse of this surah?
options: The mutual competition and boasting over the accumulation of wealth, children, and worldly possessions
The remembrance of Allah in times of ease and difficulty
The act of giving generously from one's wealth in charity
The exclusive love of a single tribe over all others
questions.explanation: Layer 1 explains that 'al-takathur' refers to the mutual competition and boasting over the accumulation of wealth, children, tribal numbers, and worldly possessions, capturing a universal human tendency to forget the purpose of life by being absorbed in amassing more.

questions.question: True or false: According to classical scholars, the historical context behind verses 1 and 2 involved two Arab tribes who competed by walking to the graveyards to count even their dead.
questions.explanation: Layer 1 records that the surah was revealed in response to two Arab tribes who competed in boasting about the size of their clans, eventually walking to the graveyards to count even their dead, an image that illustrates how deep the obsession with takathur can go.

questions.question: Which prophetic instruction does Ibn Kathir cite to connect verse 2's mention of visiting graves with a spiritual remedy?
options: 'Fast on Mondays and Thursdays, for they remind you of the Hereafter'
'I had previously forbidden you from visiting the graves, but now visit them, for they remind you of the Hereafter'
'Recite Surah al-Mulk every night before sleeping to be saved from the punishment of the grave'
'Whoever counts his dead among the boastful is not from us'
questions.explanation: Layer 2 cites Ibn Kathir quoting the hadith of the Prophet in Sahih Muslim: 'I had previously forbidden you from visiting the graves, but now visit them, for they remind you of the Hereafter,' directly connecting the Quranic instruction to a prophetic spiritual corrective.

questions.question: True or false: Ibn Kathir cites a report from Ali ibn Abi Talib stating, 'We were in doubt about the punishment of the grave until Surah al-Takathur was revealed.'
questions.explanation: Layer 2 records Ibn Kathir's citation of the report from Ali ibn Abi Talib that the companions were in doubt about the punishment of the grave until Surah al-Takathur was revealed, indicating that this surah served as decisive Quranic confirmation of the reality of barzakh punishment.

questions.question: How does Wahbah al-Zuhayli illustrate the difference between 'ilm al-yaqin' and 'ayn al-yaqin' in his commentary on this surah?
options: Like reading a book versus writing one
Like memorizing a verse versus reciting it in prayer
Like knowing fire exists because someone told you, versus seeing the fire with your own eyes
Like hearing about a city versus drawing its map
questions.explanation: Layer 3 explains that Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir uses the classical analogy: 'ilm al-yaqin' is like knowing fire exists because someone told you; 'ayn al-yaqin' is like seeing the fire with your own eyes; and 'haqq al-yaqin' is like being burnt by it.

questions.question: True or false: Sayyid Qutb argues that the Quran's promise of seeing the Hellfire is meant to be treated as merely a hypothetical, abstract theological proposition rather than a real future encounter.
questions.explanation: Layer 3 states the opposite: Sayyid Qutb argues that by describing the vision of Hellfire as a future direct, personal encounter that you will see with your own eyes, the Quran makes it impossible to treat the afterlife as merely hypothetical.

questions.question: According to the tafsir, what does 'al-na'im' (the pleasure/blessing) in the closing verse encompass?
options: Only the blessings enjoyed by the wealthy disbelievers of Quraysh
Only the spiritual rewards promised to believers in Paradise
Health, safety, sustenance, good food, water, shelter, family, and every other worldly favour
Only the obligatory acts of worship like prayer and zakat
questions.explanation: Layer 1 explains that 'al-na'im' encompasses health, safety, sustenance, good food, water, shelter, family, and every other worldly favour, with the Prophet confirming in a famous hadith that even cool shade, cool dates, and cool water are blessings about which people will be questioned.
